analysis.one_liner: Funneled all lawsuits over federal energy leasing into one court with strict 60-day filing deadlines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittees until the Congress ended; all 21 cosponsors were Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have moved every lawsuit over federal oil, gas, and energy leasing — including offshore drilling leases — into a single court, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Anyone challenging a federal leasing decision would have had 60 days to file a lawsuit or lose the right forever, and the court would have had to decide the case within 180 days or dismiss it with all rights terminated. Appeals would skip the normal appeals courts and go straight to the Supreme Court, which would also face a 180-day deadline. The bill's findings blame environmental groups whose lawsuits have delayed Arctic offshore drilling leases.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies seeking or holding federal leases: challenges to their leases would face a 60-day filing window, a single designated court, a 180-day decision deadline, and dismissal with all rights terminated if the court misses the deadline — making it much harder and slower to block or slow a lease through the courts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

how_it_helps.text: It concentrates all legal challenges to federal energy leasing decisions in the D.C. district court, which must resolve them within 180 days and prioritize them over all other cases.
It bars any claim not filed within 60 days of the federal decision, and provides that if the court misses its own 180-day deadline, the case is dismissed with prejudice and all rights are terminated.

The bill's stated purpose is to stop what it calls a 'gross abuse' of the courts by groups that have challenged Arctic offshore leases and the national offshore leasing program, which the findings say delays energy reaching the public.

analysis.who_pays: Citizens, community groups, and conservation organizations that sue over federal energy leases: they lose the ability to file in their local circuit court, face a short 60-day deadline, risk having their entire case thrown out if a crowded court misses a 180-day deadline, and lose normal appeals-court review.
analysis.who_pays_short: People and groups suing over drilling leases

drawbacks.text: A 60-day filing window can be hard for citizens and public-interest groups to meet — they must detect the federal decision, find counsel, and sue within two months or lose the right to challenge the lease forever.

If the D.C. district court does not issue a judgment within 180 days, the case is dismissed with prejudice and all rights are terminated — litigants would lose their claims entirely because of court backlog, not the merits.

Appeals would go only to the Supreme Court, bypassing the appeals courts that normally review district rulings; since the Supreme Court hears only a small share of petitions, most rulings would effectively be final with no appellate review.
Supporters would answer that litigation over offshore leases has delayed energy production at real cost to the economy, and that a fast, predictable process serves energy consumers too.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster resolution of lease disputes has some value, but the design goes well beyond speeding cases up: it eliminates normal court access for anyone harmed by a federal energy lease. The 60-day bar, the dismissal-with-prejudice rule for court delays, and the removal of appeals-court review all fall on citizens and public-interest groups while the benefits flow to leaseholders. The bill offers no fix for the delays it cites other than making most legal challenges impossible or unappealable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees where it sat until the Congress ended — it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shadegg introduced the bill on February 4, 2009, with 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

On July 23, 2009, the Judiciary Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Immigration, Citizenship, Refugees, Border Security, and International Law and the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011; the bill never received a vote in committee or on the House floor.

The bill's findings state that environmental groups have legally challenged every lease in the Alaskan Outer Continental Shelf and the entire 2007–2012 offshore leasing program, and call expedited review necessary to stop what it calls abuse of the court system.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because nothing happened. Ordinary people and conservation groups kept their full, normal access to the courts to challenge federal drilling and energy leases, and oil and gas companies did not get the single-court, fast-deadline process the bill would have created.

for.name: John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to concentrate federal energy-leasing litigation in the D.C. district court with 60-day filing and 180-day decision deadlines.

for.name: 21 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction, controlled by the Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees on July 23, 2009, and never scheduled a markup or a vote; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action beyond subcommittee referral.

industries.note: Leaseholders and prospective bidders on federal lands and offshore areas would face far fewer and faster-resolved legal challenges to their leases, with claims barred after 60 days and cases dismissed if the court misses its deadline. Their gain comes directly from narrowing ordinary people's ability to challenge drilling on public lands and waters.

The bill targets these groups' litigation directly: one designated court, a 60-day filing bar, a mandatory 180-day resolution, dismissal with rights terminated for court delay, and no appeals court review. Their ability to represent the public interest in federal leasing decisions would be sharply reduced.

industries.industry: Federal courts (D.C. district and Supreme Court)
industries.note: The bill would hand the D.C. district court exclusive jurisdiction and force its energy-leasing cases to jump ahead of all others, with dismissal sanctioned if deadlines are missed, and would require the Supreme Court to fast-track appeals ahead of all other matters. Judges gain caseload and lose scheduling discretion; the public loses the normal appeals-court layer.
